stem: When assessing for foreign body aspiration in a toddler, what is the most common radiological finding on an expiratory film?

options.text: Complete collapse of the lung distal to the object.
Increased lung volume and lucency on the affected side due to air trapping.
A large pleural effusion on the side of the aspiration.
The 'silhouette sign' obscuring the right heart border.

explanation: On expiration, the affected lung stays inflated and lucent compared to the healthy lung because the foreign body acts as a one-way valve.
rationale: Focus on what happens to trapped air when the child tries to breathe out.

optionExplanations.A: While collapse happens in adults, children more commonly experience air trapping distal to the foreign body.
optionExplanations.B: On expiration, the affected lung stays inflated and lucent compared to the healthy lung because the foreign body acts as a one-way valve.
optionExplanations.C: Pleural effusions are complications of infection like pneumonia, not the typical acute finding of foreign body aspiration.
optionExplanations.D: The silhouette sign indicates consolidation or fluid in the adjacent lung, not necessarily the air trapping found with a foreign body.

originalCorrectOptionTexts: Increased lung volume and lucency on the affected side due to air trapping.
